children.text: A three-tiered waterfall hidden in the forest of Lazi, Siquijor, where a flight of steps leads down to turquoise pools. Swimming, rope swings, and bamboo rafts all cost only a few pesos, making it the island's best-loved place to play in the water.
Cambugahay Falls is a three-tiered waterfall hidden in the forest about
2 km

from Lazi town in southeastern Siquijor, along the island's ring road. You cannot see the falls at all from the road; only after walking down the steps does the forest open up to reveal white cascades and a turquoise pool all at once, which makes the first impression unusually strong. The Siquijor provincial government's tourism guide also introduces it as the most visited attraction on the island.

The falls step down over limestone terrain from top to bottom. Some sources count more tiers, but it is usually described as having three. The pool in front of the lowest tier is the widest and deepest, and both swimming and the rope swings take place here. On clear days the water takes on a milky blue-green tint, which is said to come from dissolved limestone, and that color has long made Cambugahay the island's signature photo.

This is not a waterfall to admire from a distance; it is one you get into. The basic routine is to swim in the pool, grab a rope hung from a tree and drop into the water, and ride a bamboo raft close to the cascade. Entrance and activity fees are all small, so it is easy on the wallet, and most visitors enjoy it for an hour or two and then move on. Even people who cannot swim are often happy just to dip their feet in the shallow edge and take photos.
The overall feel of the island and the loop route are covered in the
Siquijor Island

entry, so here we focus on how to enjoy this one waterfall best. Pairing it with Lazi's old church and convent and the century-old balete tree makes a satisfying half day to full day, and it suits families with children, couples who love photos, and friends who like playing in the water.
The pool right in front of the falls is shallow at the edges and gets deeper toward the middle. Near the rope swings the water is said to be about
2 m
deep, so weaker swimmers are safest staying at the edge. The water is clear and refreshing, so it is easy to stay in for a long time.
The signature experience here is grabbing a rope hung from a tree and dropping into the pool. The fee is usually about
per rope with unlimited turns on that rope, but some places charge separately for different ropes, so ask before you go.
You sit on a raft of lashed bamboo and are taken close to the falling water. The fee is said to be about
, and photos taken in the spray in front of the falls are popular.
From the roadside you walk down about 130–150 steps to the falls. The moment the sound of water grows louder through the trees and the view suddenly opens up is one of the highlights of the visit.

blocks.title: Exploring the rocky path to the upper tiers

children.text: Past the lowest tier, a rocky path leads upward to shallow channels lined with bamboo railings and small pools. There are fewer people than below and the trickling water has a different mood, but the mossy rocks are slippery, so wear shoes and walk slowly.

blocks.title: Light in the early morning and late afternoon

children.text: Early in the morning, before the tour groups arrive, you can almost have the pool to yourself and the water looks clear. Late in the afternoon the light is soft and gives the falls warm tones in photos, but the rope swings usually close around 5:00 PM.

blocks.title: A break at the entrance stalls

children.text: Near the entrance there are small shops selling coconuts, drinks, and snacks. Climbing back up wet and resting with a cold coconut has become the traditional way to end the visit. There is no proper restaurant, so eat in Lazi town.

items.title: Half-day route (early morning visit)
items.subtitle: Based on a San Juan stay

children.text: Leave your San Juan accommodation by motorbike or tricycle and ride about
40 minutes
along the ring road
Arrive at opening time, park, and pay the entrance fee at the gate
Walk down the steps to the lowest tier and take wide shots while no one is around
Swim in the pool and try the rope swing, plus the bamboo raft if you like
Explore the rocky path and the bamboo-railed path on the upper tiers
Finish before the tour groups pile in, climb back up the steps, and change clothes
Head into Lazi town to see the church and convent
Midday sunlight makes the water color look sharpest but is also when it is most crowded. If photos are your goal, between 8 and 9 AM is a good compromise.

items.title: Full-day route (Lazi area and the east coast)
items.subtitle: Combines the falls with Lazi's sights

children.text: Swim and use the rope swing at Cambugahay Falls
See Lazi Church and the convent across the road
The century-old balete tree in Campalanas and its fish spa
Lunch at a simple eatery in Lazi town
Photos riding the broomstick at Hapitanan and the view
Ride east along the ring road to Maria and visit Kagusuan Beach or Salagdoong Beach
Return to San Juan or Siquijor town before dark

This route sweeps the southeast of the island from Lazi to Maria in one pass, so it is most efficient by motorbike. There are almost no streetlights on the way back to San Juan on the west side, so set off before it gets dark.
From Manila, fly to Dumaguete-Sibulan Airport (DGT) in about
1 hour 20 minutes
. From the airport, take a tricycle or taxi to Dumaguete port, then board a boat to Siquijor port. The regular ferry takes about
2 hours
and costs about
, while fast boats take around
1 hour
and cost more. From Cebu, Sunlight Air flies direct to Siquijor Airport, but flight days change often, so check the latest notice.
How to reach the island from the port and airport, and the ferry timetables by carrier, are covered in the
Siquijor Island
entry.
From Siquijor port (Siquijor town) to the falls is about
along the island's ring road, and about
30–40 minutes
by tricycle. A one-way fare is bargained and is about
. A round trip with the driver waiting, or a full-day charter that also covers the Lazi area, is usually more economical, and drivers ask about
for that.
You can rent a motorbike at the port or at San Juan accommodations for about
a day, with fuel extra. From Siquijor port to the falls takes about
30 minutes
, and from San Juan about
40 minutes
. The ring road is well paved with little traffic, so it is easy even for first-timers, but you need a motorbike license (an international permit counts) and a helmet.
At the falls parking area, motorbike parking is about
and tricycle parking is about
If you stay in Lazi town, the falls are about
10 minutes
away by tricycle or motorbike. Staying in Lazi is the best choice for anyone who wants to arrive first thing in the morning. From the roadside you walk down a stepped path to the falls.
There are day tours from Dumaguete that combine the falls with the island's heritage sights. They are said to cost about

per person, and since time at the falls is short, only an hour or two, an overnight stay is better if you want to play longer. Check the operator's latest notice for what is included and the current price.
The best time for Cambugahay is the dry season,
November–May
. With little rain the water stays a clear turquoise and the steps are less slippery. In the late dry season,
April–May
, the flow shrinks, the cascades thin out, and the color may fade, so if you want the fullest water,
December–February
is better.
In the rainy season,
June–October

, showers come in short, frequent bursts and the flow grows more impressive, but after heavy rain the water turns muddy brown and the paths become slippery, so swimming may be restricted. When a weather warning goes up, boats to and from Dumaguete can be cancelled, so leave slack in your schedule in the rainy season. Weekends, public holidays, and Holy Week are crowded with domestic visitors, so a weekday morning is recommended.

rows: Clear water and a good flow — the best-balanced period

The closest town to the falls is Lazi. It is a quiet town with a church and convent and fewer places to stay, but at about
10 minutes
from the falls it is the most convenient base for an early morning visit. Most travelers stay in San Juan, on the southwest of the island where restaurants and dive shops gather, and ride about
40 minutes
to the falls. In San Juan, rooms with a fan and shared bathroom cost about
a night, air-conditioned guesthouses with private bathrooms about
, and mid-range beachfront resorts about

The entrance has nothing but stalls selling coconuts, drinks, and snacks, and no restaurant, so people usually eat at a simple eatery in Lazi town. Siquijor's typical grilled coastal fish and coconut dishes can be found in San Juan and Siquijor town. Swimming makes you hungry, so bring snacks before you go, and carry a large towel you can sit on in wet clothes.
Arrive at opening time,
. After
tour groups arrive and the pool starts to get crowded.
The steps and rocks are slippery, so wear water shoes or sandals with good grip, and avoid flip-flops.
Collectors may charge anywhere from
to
for entry depending on who is at the gate, so bring small bills and coins under
. There is no ATM on site.
Before using a rope swing, check the fee and any limit on turns. Many places allow unlimited turns for about
per rope.
Put your phone and camera in a waterproof pouch, and bring dry clothes to change into and a large towel.
For a wide shot, stand on the far edge of the lowest tier and fit all three streams in one frame. For the upper tiers, the bamboo-railed path is a good vantage point.
It is said there is no official ban on drones, but that does not mean permission has been given. Ask the collector at the entrance first, and follow national aviation rules too.
A late afternoon visit is quiet and the light is good, but the rope swings finish around
and you still have to climb the steps, so head out before dark.
There are reports that no lifeguard is on duty. Children and weaker swimmers should stay in the shallow edge next to a guardian.
The water at the rope swing is about
2 m
deep. Before you jump, check that no one is below, and after landing move aside right away to give the next person room.
You go up and down about 130–150 steps between the road and the falls. Climbing out wet leaves you short of breath, so people with weak knees and older visitors should rest along the way.
There are reports that the fee varies from free up to
depending on who collects it. Check the fee schedule or ticket and pay the exact amount in small bills.
Keep your belongings where you can see them and leave valuables at your accommodation. When you play in the pool, someone needs to keep an eye on the bags.
To keep the pool clear, do not put on a lot of sunscreen right before getting in, and take all your trash back with you.
Right after heavy rain, the current suddenly gets stronger, the water turns muddy, and the steps and rocks become very slippery. If the local staff tell you not to swim, follow them without fail.
In Lazi town, about
2 km

from the falls, stands San Isidro Labrador Church, built in the 1880s, and across the road is an old convent building said to be among the largest in Asia. Inside the church, the old hardwood floor is still preserved.

This balete (banyan) tree in Campalanas is several hundred years old, with a spring welling up beneath its roots into a small pool, famous for a fish spa where small fish nibble your feet. It is about
6–8 km
from the falls and the entrance fee is about
Another waterfall in Lazi, reached by walking about
15 minutes
down a forest trail to a small cascade and a wide pool. It has a rope swing and a rock slide, and the entrance fee is said to be about
A small island with a ring road of about
72 km
and six municipalities. Besides the falls it has sunset beaches, caves, and traditional healing culture, so it is easy to combine into a one-day motorbike loop.
The most common gateway city to Siquijor, about
1–1.5 hours
away by boat. With an airport, hotels, and restaurants, it is a good place to spend a night before or after the island.
